Data Anonymization Methods: On Data Protection
Reviewing and Understanding the Common Methods for Anonymizing Information
While learning about data minimization techniques in the Udacity course, the following questions came to mind: What are anonymization techniques? What are they? Can they be classified? And how do they relate to minimization techniques? While searching for answers, I reached the following conclusions:
•
The terms “minimization techniques” and “anonymization techniques” can be synonymous; but only in the technical context of transforming data with a privacy focus. Privacy is about using data to the minimum extent necessary.
•
The term “minimization techniques” can also be used to refer to techniques employed in the data minimization process: the process of limiting the stored data useful for the software’s operation[2].
With these topics clarified, a definition I found for data anonymization was the following: “the process of removing identification from sensitive data while preserving its data type and format”[1].
With this concept, we see that these methods follow privacy guidelines; but they are not necessarily the same: privacy seeks to preserve the efficiency of data use to the minimum possible extent; but anonymization is generally not obligated to do so, instead eliminating it entirely. This difference can also be referred to as pseudoanonymization[8], which groups certain methods like masking or encryption[9] or any type of replacement.
“Privacy and/or pseudoanonymization methods seek the minimally efficient use of sensitive data, while anonymization methods seek to erase all traces of it.”
Criteria for Classifying Techniques
Each technique within anonymization methods has categories that indicate what the method does and its benefits and limitations. The categories span the type of data; the approach and the anonymization objective[3].
In the nature or type of data, it’s not just tabular or textual information, but also connectivity; also called graph; and sets of items associated with the user. The approach of an anonymization technique generally falls into 4 points:
•
Generalization: grouping attributes into representative groups of their value.
•
Suppression: hiding the full or partial value of the attribute[5].
•
Perturbation: adding some type of noise and/or extra value to the attribute to generate a new one.
•
Permutation: grouping attributes into groups and shuffling them internally within each group[5].
•
Anatomization: separating sensitive attributes from those rarely used to identify the user[5].
Anonymization objectives aim to reduce the ability to infer or discover the association of information with the user’s identity; thus proposing a model based on the information the attacker has about the user:
•
K-anonymity: placing at least K individuals with a common sensitive attribute into an equivalent group.
•
L-diversity: ensuring L diversity of values for a group with a common sensitive attribute; such that each group has at least L options.
•
T-closeness: indicating that the distance of an attribute’s distribution within a group compared to the distribution in the table does not exceed the value of T.
These objectives can be grouped into a higher category called syntactic privacy or anonymization; which seeks to generate a new value based on a “syntactic property” of the attribute to hinder identification[3].
Common Techniques for Anonymization
While there are different types of data that can be used; the most common is the tabular approach for most companies when modeling their businesses. In this section, I’ll include both privacy/pseudoanonymization and anonymization methods.
Generalization
Replaces a value with a member of a bounded range set that contains the value[7]; this allows controlling multiple levels of precision over the type of range associated with the value. It is an approach for generalization.
Swapping or swapping
Reorganizes all values within an attribute in a table so that it no longer resembles the original version. This erases the relationship between an attribute and the individual, generating anonymization for the record[4]. It is an approach for permutation.
Masking
Replaces segments of the value using a specific symbol, usually *; or random characters for each segment member[4]. This allows manipulating the attribute for identification without exposing it[8]. It is an approach for suppression.
Perturbation
By applying “rounding” formulas and adding random noise to the original value, a new value is created. One must be careful with this: if the changes are too small, it may not anonymize much; but if the changes are too large, precision in the data is lost[7]. Rounding methods are ways to give an “exact” value to an “approximate” value. It is an approach for perturbation.
Encryption
Using some encryption method; whether ciphering or hashing; a new value is created[8]. Used to preserve the truthfulness of data by replicating it with a possible candidate. It is an approach for suppression.
Shuffling
Randomly swaps the segments that make up the value so that it is no longer recognizable[8]. It is an approach for permutation.
Blurring
Uses approximate values as a replacement for the original value, such that precision is lost to some degree[8], generally applied to numbers. It is an approach for generalization.
Pseudonymization
Replaces the real value with a fake value or pseudonym in full or partial form; preserving the integration of the attached data along with the common row’s statistical distribution, allowing it to be used for testing and analysis[4]. It is an approach for suppression.
Conclusion
The topic of data anonymization is a crucial part of delivering privacy to the different types of stakeholders or interested parties in our environment. Knowing the most common anonymization algorithms and their properties will help us know how to use them in our privacy challenges, and thus create better programs for it within our systems.
